questions.text: The business has a written plan for the next 12 months that sets sales and profit targets.
anchors: No plan exists; direction is only in the owner's head
Owner can describe goals verbally but nothing is written
Written plan lists activities but has no numbers for sales or profit
Written plan states sales and profit targets in cedis
Written plan with targets, updated within the last 12 months with changes recorded

evidence.requirement: Ask to see the current plan and check it has numeric targets and a date of last update.
examples: Business plan or annual plan document
Notebook page with dated sales and profit targets

questions.text: Staff who run sales, production or service can state the current target for their own area.
anchors: No targets exist for any area of the business
Owner has targets in mind but staff do not know them
Some staff can state a target when asked
All staff in charge of an area can state their target
All can state their target and the latest result against it

evidence.requirement: Ask two or three staff or helpers, separately, what their target is and how they are doing against it.
examples: Shop attendant states daily sales target
Production lead states weekly output target and last week's result

questions.text: Before any large spend on equipment, stock or expansion, the owner writes down the cost, the expected extra income and the payback time.
anchors: Large purchases are made on impulse with no calculation
Owner thinks about the benefit but writes nothing down
Cost is written but expected return is not
Cost, expected extra income and payback time are written for the last large spend
Written for every large spend in 12 months and actual results later compared

evidence.requirement: Ask for the calculation behind the last large purchase or expansion and check it was done before the spend.
examples: Page showing machine cost, extra sales expected and months to recover cost
Quotation with owner's handwritten payback calculation

questions.text: The business has customers who come back to buy again, and the records can show this.
anchors: No repeat buyers, or no sales record that could show any
Owner says some customers return but cannot name any
Owner can name three to five repeat customers
Records show more than five customers who bought in at least two of the last six months
Repeat customers account for over half of sales and repeat orders grew over the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Check sales records for the same customers buying in different months and ask two customers by phone.
examples: Mobile money history with repeat payers

questions.text: In the last 12 months the business changed a product, service or delivery method because customers told it what they wanted.
anchors: Never asks customers and has changed nothing
Hears complaints but changes nothing
Asked customers once and noted views without acting
Made one change after customer feedback and can say what it was
Made several changes from feedback and checked sales or satisfaction afterwards

evidence.requirement: Ask for a specific change, its date and the feedback behind it, and check with a customer if possible.
examples: New pack size after buyers asked for smaller units
Opening hours changed after customer survey notes

questions.text: The business can say clearly why customers choose it over a competitor, and customers give the same reason when asked.
anchors: Cannot say why customers choose it
Gives only a general reason such as good quality or low price
Gives one specific reason but customers have not confirmed it
Gives a specific reason and two of three customers called give the same one
Specific reason confirmed by customers and used in the business's selling or marketing

evidence.requirement: Ask the owner for the reason, then ask three customers why they buy from the business.
examples: Customers say the business delivers same day
Banner or social media post stating the main reason

questions.text: A written plan says how and where new customers will be found this year.
anchors: No plan to find new customers
Owner has ideas but nothing is written
Written list of ideas with no person or dates
Written plan with actions, a responsible person and dates
Written plan, actions carried out and the number of new customers recorded

evidence.requirement: Ask to see the plan and the count of new customers won against it.
examples: Notebook list of target buyers with visit dates

questions.text: The business keeps a list of customer names and phone numbers and uses it to reach customers directly.
anchors: No customer list exists
Numbers are only on the owner's phone and are not used
A list exists but is used rarely
List is kept up to date and used at least monthly, for example a WhatsApp broadcast list
List includes purchase history and is used for targeted offers with results noted

evidence.requirement: Ask to see the list and a recent message or call log showing how it was used.
examples: Spreadsheet of customers and last purchase

questions.text: Share of sales in the last 12 months that came from the single largest customer.
anchors: Above 60 percent, or the share is not known
41 to 60 percent
31 to 40 percent
16 to 30 percent
15 percent or less

evidence.requirement: Calculate the largest customer's share from the sales ledger, invoices or payment history.
examples: Invoice register for the last 12 months

questions.text: The business knows which way of reaching customers (referral, shop location, WhatsApp, social media, radio, agents) brings the most new customers.
anchors: No deliberate marketing and no idea how customers arrive
Does some marketing but has no idea which part works
Owner estimates the best channel from memory
Asks new customers how they heard and has counts for the last three months
Counts new customers by channel monthly and has moved effort or money to the best channel

evidence.requirement: Ask for counts of new customers by source and an example of a decision based on them.
examples: Tally of 'how did you hear about us' answers
Social media page insights with enquiry counts

questions.text: The price of each main product or service is set from its cost plus a target margin.
anchors: Prices are guessed or copied without any cost calculation
Prices follow competitors only; cost is not worked out
Cost is roughly worked out for the main items only
Prices come from a written cost plus margin for all main items
As before, and the sheet is dated and updated at least twice a year or when input costs change

evidence.requirement: Ask for the costing sheet behind two main prices and check the date.
examples: Costing sheet with ingredients, labour, transport and margin
Spreadsheet with cost and selling price per item

questions.text: How often does the owner check competitors' prices and offers?
anchors: Never checks competitors
Rarely, only when customers complain about price
Sometimes, about once a year, from memory
Often, at least every six months, with notes
Always, every quarter, in a written comparison used when setting prices

evidence.requirement: Ask when the last check was done and for any notes or comparison.
examples: Notebook of competitor prices with dates

questions.text: Discounts and price reductions are given under a rule, not case by case on request.
anchors: Discounts are given freely with no limit
Owner decides case by case and nothing is recorded
An informal limit exists that only the owner knows
A written rule exists and sales staff know it
Written rule applied, discounts recorded and their total cost reviewed monthly

evidence.requirement: Ask for the discount rule and a record of discounts given last month.
examples: Sales book with a discount column

questions.text: Orders are delivered on the agreed day and to the agreed specification.
anchors: Orders are often late or wrong and no record is kept
More than one in five orders is late or wrong, according to customers
Orders are sometimes late or wrong and this is not tracked
Orders are rarely late or wrong and late orders are noted
On-time and correct rate is tracked monthly and is above 90 percent

evidence.requirement: Ask two buyers about reliability and check any delivery or order log.
examples: Buyer confirms deliveries arrive on time
Delivery book with dates promised and dates delivered

questions.text: Products or work are checked against a stated standard before they reach the customer.
anchors: No checks are done
Checks happen only when the owner is present
Checks are usually done but nothing is written
A written checklist exists and is used for most sales or jobs
Checklist is used for every batch or job, failures are recorded and causes fixed

evidence.requirement: Observe a check being done and look at the checklist and failure records.
examples: Quality checklist at the packing table

questions.text: Customer complaints, returns and refunds are written down and followed up.
anchors: Complaints are ignored or not handled
Complaints are handled informally and forgotten
The owner remembers complaints but nothing is written
A written log exists with the action taken
Log records cause and action, complaints are closed within an agreed time and patterns reviewed

evidence.requirement: Ask to see the complaints or returns log for the last three months.
examples: WhatsApp complaint messages with replies and outcome

questions.text: The main products or services are made or delivered by following set steps, so different staff produce the same result.
anchors: Every person does the work their own way and results differ widely
Only the owner knows the right way
Steps are shown to new staff by demonstration but not written
Steps are written or illustrated for the main product or service
Steps are written, staff are trained on them and they were updated in the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Watch two staff do the same task and compare with any written steps.
examples: Recipe or production sheet on the wall
Step list for a standard repair or service

questions.text: Stock, materials or supplies on hand are physically counted and compared with the stock records.
anchors: Stock is never counted
Counted once a year or only when a problem appears
Counted every two to three months
Counted every month and compared with records
Counted every month, differences investigated and the cause recorded

evidence.requirement: Observe or ask for the latest count sheet and the record it was compared with.
examples: Stock count sheet signed by two people
Stock book with count date and variance column

questions.text: Each key input or item for resale can be bought from at least two known suppliers.
anchors: Depends on one supplier and knows no alternative
One main supplier; alternatives have never been checked
An alternative supplier is named but has not been used
Two suppliers have been used in the last six months for each key input
As before, and prices from suppliers are compared in writing at least twice a year

evidence.requirement: Review purchase records for each key input and ask for alternative supplier contacts.
examples: Purchase book showing two suppliers per item

questions.text: Waste, spoilage, breakage or loss is measured as a share of what is bought or produced.
anchors: Not measured and the owner cannot estimate it
Estimated from memory only
Recorded occasionally for the main item
Recorded every month for the main items
Recorded monthly with causes noted, and losses are falling or below a set target

evidence.requirement: Ask for loss records and check how the percentage is worked out.
examples: Production sheet showing input quantity and good output

questions.text: Each month the main cost lines (inputs, transport, power, rent, wages) are compared with the previous month and rises are explained.
anchors: Costs are never compared
Costs are looked at only when cash runs short
Owner notices big changes informally
Main cost lines are compared monthly and rises are queried
Compared monthly against a budget or target and corrective action is recorded

evidence.requirement: Ask for the last two months' cost comparison and the action taken on any rise.
examples: Notebook comparing fuel and input costs

questions.text: Equipment and vehicles are serviced on a planned schedule rather than only after they break down.
anchors: Repairs only after breakdown
Servicing happens when someone remembers
Informal schedule for the main items
Written schedule for main assets and mostly followed
Schedule followed, service log kept and breakdown time recorded

evidence.requirement: Ask for the service schedule and log and inspect one key machine or vehicle.

questions.text: The business keeps a list of its equipment and other assets with purchase cost, date and condition.
anchors: No list exists
The owner lists assets only from memory
A list of main items exists without values
A list shows cost, purchase date, condition and location
List is checked physically at least yearly and updated, with serial or chassis numbers

evidence.requirement: Ask for the asset list and tick three items from the list at the premises.
examples: Spreadsheet of machines with purchase receipts attached

questions.text: Output or work completed per worker or per day is measured for the main product or service.
anchors: Not measured
Estimated from memory
Counted occasionally
Counted every week for the main product or service
Counted routinely, compared with a target and acted on

evidence.requirement: Ask for output counts for the last four weeks and any target.

questions.text: The main work process has no regular bottleneck that delays orders.
anchors: Orders are delayed every day by the same problem
Orders are delayed weekly and nothing is done
The bottleneck is known but there is no plan to fix it
The bottleneck is known and a fix is in progress
The bottleneck is solved, or capacity is checked each quarter against orders

evidence.requirement: Walk the process with the owner and ask what slows orders most and what has been done.
examples: Single dryer or machine causing queues
Order backlog list with reasons for delay

questions.text: All cash and mobile money received and paid out is written in a cash book or other record every week.
anchors: No record of money in or out is kept
Only some sales are noted and not regularly
Receipts and payments are recorded but more than a month behind
Cash and mobile money in and out are recorded at least weekly
Recorded daily and checked weekly against cash on hand and the mobile money or bank balance

evidence.requirement: Inspect the cash book or spreadsheet for the last eight weeks and check entry dates against statements.
examples: Spreadsheet matching mobile money statement entries

questions.text: Business money is kept separate from the owner's household and personal money.
anchors: Business and personal money are in the same pocket, wallet or account
Sometimes separate, but the owner takes cash freely with no record
Separate account or wallet exists but personal use still happens and is not recorded
Separate money, and the owner's withdrawals are recorded as drawings or salary
Separate accounts, a fixed monthly owner pay, and no unrecorded personal withdrawals in the last three months

evidence.requirement: Review three months of bank and mobile money statements for personal spending and compare with drawings records.
examples: Business account statement with only business payments
Drawings page in the cash book

questions.text: Sales and purchases are recorded in a ledger or software with the date, amount and the customer or supplier.
anchors: No ledger exists
Receipts and invoices are kept loosely but not recorded
Sales are recorded but purchases are not
Both sales and purchases are recorded with dates, amounts and names
As before, and monthly totals agree with bank and mobile money statements

evidence.requirement: Sample ten entries and trace them to receipts, invoices or statements.

questions.text: Receipts, invoices and waybills are filed so that any transaction in the last 12 months can be traced.
anchors: No supporting documents are kept
Some are kept loose and unsorted
Kept in a box or bag but not sorted by date
Filed by month and can be found when asked
Filed and cross-referenced to ledger entries; five random transactions are found within ten minutes

evidence.requirement: Pick five ledger entries at random and ask for the supporting document for each.
examples: Scanned invoices stored by date in a cloud folder

questions.text: Weeks of fixed costs (rent, wages, loan repayments, power, transport) that cash on hand and in accounts could pay today.
anchors: Less than 1 week of fixed costs, or the balance is not known
1 week to under 2 weeks
2 weeks to under 4 weeks
4 weeks to under 8 weeks
8 weeks or more

evidence.requirement: Add cash, bank and mobile money balances on the day and divide by weekly fixed costs from the records.
examples: Bank and mobile money balances shown on the day

questions.text: A written cash forecast shows the money expected in and out over the coming weeks.
anchors: No forecast of any kind
Owner thinks about upcoming cash but writes nothing
A list of big upcoming payments only
A written four week forecast updated at least monthly
A rolling 13 week forecast updated every two weeks and compared with actual results

evidence.requirement: Ask for the current forecast and the last update date.
examples: Four week cash plan in a notebook

questions.text: Average number of days customers take to pay on credit sales.
anchors: Not known, or more than 60 days
46 to 60 days
31 to 45 days
16 to 30 days
15 days or fewer

evidence.requirement: Compute from the list of unpaid invoices and recent payment dates.
examples: Debtors list with invoice and payment dates

questions.text: The gross margin (sales less direct cost) is known for each main product or service.
anchors: Not known at all
Owner guesses an overall margin
Calculated once for the whole business in the last year
Calculated for each main product or service in the last six months
Calculated for each main item every month and used in decisions

evidence.requirement: Ask for the margin calculation for the top three items and check it uses real costs.

questions.text: The monthly sales needed to cover all costs (break-even) has been calculated.
anchors: Never heard of break-even and not calculated
Owner has a vague idea of what sales are needed
Rough estimate not based on records
Calculated from fixed and variable costs in the last 12 months
Calculated and compared with actual sales every month

evidence.requirement: Ask for the calculation and check the fixed and variable costs used.
examples: Notebook page listing fixed costs and margin

questions.text: Net profit or loss after all costs, including the owner's own pay, has been worked out for the last 12 months.
anchors: Never worked out
Owner estimates profit by feel
Estimated from bank or mobile money movement only
Worked out from records but without the owner's pay
Worked out from records after owner's pay and tax, and the figure agrees with the books

evidence.requirement: Ask for the profit calculation and check it against the ledger totals.

questions.text: Financial statements (income statement and balance sheet) have been prepared for the last full year.
anchors: No financial statements have ever been prepared
Owner has written a rough summary only
A one page profit summary exists without a balance sheet
Full statements prepared for the last year by the owner or a bookkeeper
Statements prepared for the last two years and reviewed or audited by an external accountant

evidence.requirement: Ask for the statements and check they cover a full year and balance.
examples: Annual accounts prepared by an accountant

questions.text: Payments above a set limit need approval from someone other than the person asking for the money.
anchors: Anyone can pay out money freely
The owner approves in theory but not in practice
The owner approves verbally with no record
A written limit exists and a named person approves above it
Written limit, approvals are recorded and the owner checks them monthly

evidence.requirement: Ask for the limit and look at three recent large payments for approval evidence.
examples: Approval message on WhatsApp saved with the receipt

questions.text: Cash, bank and mobile money balances are reconciled to the business records at least monthly.
anchors: Never reconciled
Only when an error is suspected
Done about once a quarter
Done every month by the owner
Done every month by someone who does not record the money, with differences explained in writing

evidence.requirement: Ask for the last three reconciliations and compare with statements.
examples: Cash count sheet matched to cash book and MoMo balance

questions.text: All loans and supplier credit are repaid on or before the due date.
anchors: Currently in default or in arrears of more than 90 days
Late payments in the last 12 months with penalties charged
One or two late payments in the last 12 months, no penalties
All repayments on time in the last 12 months, shown by statements
All repayments on time for 24 months with written repayment schedules

evidence.requirement: Review loan statements or lender letters and supplier statements for the last 12 months.

questions.text: Monthly cash available before loan repayments compared with the monthly loan repayments (debt cover).
anchors: Below 1.0 times, or not known
1.0 to under 1.2 times
1.2 to under 1.5 times
1.5 to under 2.0 times
2.0 times or more

evidence.requirement: Divide average monthly cash surplus before debt payments by monthly repayments using records.
examples: Cash book summary and loan schedule

questions.riskTag: Loan repayments not covered by cash

questions.text: The business keeps an up to date list of everything it owes (loans, supplier balances, advances) with amounts and due dates.
anchors: No list of debts exists
The owner knows the debts from memory only
A list of loans exists but not supplier balances
All debts are listed with amounts and due dates and updated monthly
List updated monthly and checked against lender and supplier statements

evidence.requirement: Ask for the list and check three items against a statement.
examples: Loan schedule and supplier balances sheet

questions.text: Borrowed money is used for stock, equipment or other items that earn income, not for routine shortfalls or personal spending.
anchors: Loans mostly pay for personal or routine bills
Sometimes used for personal or routine bills
Mixed use, not tracked
Used mainly for income earning items, shown by receipts
Each loan has a written purpose and expected return before it is taken, and use was verified

evidence.requirement: Trace the last loan's use through receipts and records.
examples: Receipts for equipment bought with a loan
Loan application stating purpose, matched to spending

questions.text: The business and its owner have no unresolved loan default, court judgement or blacklisting with a lender or credit bureau.
anchors: In default or blacklisted now
Arrears or a dispute is currently being renegotiated
A past default has been fully cleared and the owner can show proof
No default is known but this has not been checked with a bureau
No default, confirmed by a credit report obtained in the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Ask for a credit report and lender clearance letters for any past default.
examples: Lender letter confirming a loan is fully repaid

questions.text: The owner has obtained a copy of their own credit report from a licensed credit bureau and checked it for errors.
anchors: Has never heard of credit bureaus
Knows bureaus exist but has not asked for a report
Requested a report but did not review it
Obtained and reviewed a report in the last 24 months
Obtained a report in the last 12 months and challenged any errors in writing

evidence.requirement: Ask to see the report and any dispute letter to the bureau.

questions.text: The business or owner saves regularly in a bank, susu or VSLA for planned business needs.
anchors: No regular saving
Saves only occasionally
Saves regularly but the money is mixed with personal funds
Regular business saving in a separate account or group for at least six months
Saved for 12 months or more and used for planned purchases or to part fund a loan, with records

evidence.requirement: Ask for savings statements or the susu or VSLA book showing contributions.

questions.text: The business has prepared and submitted a complete loan, grant or investment application in the last three years.
anchors: Has never applied
Applied but the application was incomplete or missing documents
Submitted one complete application and kept no feedback
Submitted a complete application and kept the lender or funder feedback
Submitted more than one, used the feedback to improve, and at least one succeeded

evidence.requirement: Ask for copies of applications and decision or feedback letters.

questions.text: A written funding plan states how much money is needed, for what, from which source and by when.
anchors: No funding plan
An amount is in the owner's mind but not written
Amount and purpose are written without a source
Amount, purpose, source and timing are written and costed
As before, with supplier quotations and projected repayment or returns

evidence.requirement: Ask for the funding plan and supporting quotations.
examples: Quotation for equipment with a funding table

questions.text: The business can show financial projections for the next 12 to 36 months with the assumptions written down.
anchors: No projections
Only a growth target without figures
Sales projection only, without costs
A 12 month projection of sales, costs and profit with assumptions
A three year projection, monthly in year one, with assumptions compared with actual results

evidence.requirement: Ask for the projection and check that its assumptions are stated and plausible.
examples: Spreadsheet projection with an assumptions sheet

questions.text: Who owns the business, and in what shares, is written down and can be shown.
anchors: Ownership is unclear or disputed
Only a verbal understanding exists
Owners are known informally but nothing is written
Ownership is recorded in a signed document or registration record
As before, and the ownership filed with the Registrar General is up to date

evidence.requirement: Ask for registration papers, partnership deed or shareholder records and check names match.

questions.text: The owner can put together a funder information pack (records, statements and registration documents) within one working day.
anchors: Cannot be assembled
Could be assembled within a week with great effort
Could be assembled within two to three days
Could be assembled within one day but is not kept together
A ready folder, on paper or digital, was updated within the last six months

evidence.requirement: Ask the owner to produce the pack now and time it.
examples: Digital folder with certificates, statements and ledger summary
Box file with up to date documents

questions.text: The business can run for a week without the owner on site, with sales and daily decisions continuing.
anchors: The business stops or fails when the owner is away
Major activities stop and customers are turned away
Routine work continues but every decision waits for the owner
Routine work and daily decisions are handled by a named deputy for a week
This has happened in the last 12 months with no loss, and a written handover was used

evidence.requirement: Ask staff and the deputy what happens when the owner travels or is ill and when it last occurred.
examples: Deputy describes decisions taken during owner's absence
Handover note from the owner's last trip

questions.text: A deputy or successor for the owner's role has been named in writing.
anchors: No one has been considered
The owner intends to name someone but has not
Someone is named verbally and known to staff or family
A successor or deputy is named in a signed or dated document
Named in writing, briefed on key accounts and contacts, and has already acted in the role

evidence.requirement: Ask for the document and interview the named person.
examples: Board or family meeting minutes naming a successor

questions.text: How often does the owner set aside time to work on the business (planning, review, improving), not only in it?
anchors: Never; all time goes on daily tasks
Rarely, only in a crisis
Sometimes, about once a month
Often, a weekly slot in the diary
Always, a weekly slot with decisions or actions recorded

evidence.requirement: Ask for the diary or notes showing the planning time and what was decided.
examples: Diary entry blocking Friday review time

questions.text: In the last 12 months the owner changed a business practice after training, coaching or advice.
anchors: No training or advice received and none sought
Attended training but changed nothing
Attended and tried one idea once
Changed one practice and still uses it
Changed several practices and measured the result

evidence.requirement: Ask for the practice changed, the date, and evidence it is still used.
examples: New cash book started after a bookkeeping workshop
Pricing sheet introduced after coaching visit

questions.text: Every person's role and who they report to is written down.
anchors: No roles are defined
Roles are only understood verbally
Written for some roles
Written for all roles and known to staff
Written, signed by staff and reviewed within the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Ask for role descriptions or an organisation chart and check staff know theirs.
examples: Simple organisation chart on the wall

questions.applies: Has two or more people working in the business

questions.text: People working in the business (staff, apprentices, helpers) are trained for their jobs when they join and when their tasks change.
anchors: No training is given
People learn by watching and there is no plan
A basic induction is given to some people
Induction for all new people and training when tasks change, recorded
Annual training plan with a budget, and results checked against performance

evidence.requirement: Ask for induction or training records and ask two people what training they received.
examples: Induction checklist signed by the new worker

questions.text: People who perform well are recognised or rewarded in a clear and fair way.
anchors: Same pay and no recognition whatever the performance
Rewards go to favourites
Occasional bonuses decided by the owner
Criteria for rewards are known to staff and applied
Written reward scheme with criteria, applied and reviewed each year

evidence.requirement: Ask two staff how rewards are decided and ask for the criteria and recent examples.
examples: Staff describe how the best seller was rewarded

questions.text: The business knows how many people left in the last 12 months and why.
anchors: No idea how many have left
The owner recalls some leavers
Count is known but not the reasons
Count and reasons are recorded
Recorded, and action was taken on a repeated reason

evidence.requirement: Ask for the leaver list and reasons, and the action taken on any pattern.
examples: Staff register with leaving dates and reasons

questions.text: How often does the owner meet staff or the management team to review sales, costs, cash and actions?
anchors: Never
Rarely, only when there is a problem
Quarterly
Monthly
Monthly with written minutes and actions followed up

evidence.requirement: Ask for minutes or an action list from the last three meetings.
examples: WhatsApp group summary of monthly review

questions.text: Someone outside the business and the owner's family (adviser, mentor, board member) regularly challenges major decisions.
anchors: No outside person is consulted
Occasional chats with a friend
An adviser is consulted occasionally on major decisions
An advisory group or board meets at least twice a year
Meets quarterly with minutes, tracked actions and at least one independent member

evidence.requirement: Ask for minutes or advice notes and interview the adviser.

questions.text: Staff know in writing which decisions they can make without asking the owner (spending, pricing, hiring, discounts).
anchors: The owner decides everything and nothing is stated
Staff guess what they may decide
Verbal limits are given for some decisions
Written limits exist for spending, pricing and hiring
Written limits signed by staff and reviewed within the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Ask for the written limits and ask two staff what they can decide alone.

questions.text: Employees have a written statement of their job, pay, hours and leave.
anchors: No written terms for anyone
Terms are verbal only
Written for some staff, for example only senior staff
Written for all permanent staff
Written for all staff, signed by both sides, copy held by the worker, and pay and leave records match

evidence.requirement: Sample three employee contracts or statements and check pay and leave records.
examples: Appointment letter with pay and leave terms

questions.text: Basic safety measures are in place for the main hazards of the work.
anchors: Obvious hazards are uncontrolled
Hazards are known but nothing is done
Some measures exist, such as a first aid box, without a routine
Measures are in place for each main hazard, for example first aid, fire safety and protective gear
As before, with incidents recorded and safety checks done at least quarterly

evidence.requirement: Walk the premises and check safety items, and ask for any incident record.
examples: First aid box and fire extinguisher with service date

questions.text: Registration certificates, licences, permits, leases, contracts and insurance papers are kept together in one safe place.
anchors: Papers are scattered or lost
Some are held but the owner does not know where all are
Most are at the owner's home or shop with no copies
All are in one place with a list of what is held
In one place with scanned copies kept elsewhere, and the list is updated yearly

evidence.requirement: Ask the owner to produce three named documents and the list.
examples: Lever arch file of legal documents

questions.text: Every sale of value is supported by an invoice, receipt or order note that the business keeps a copy of.
anchors: No sales documents are issued
Issued only when the customer asks
Issued for some sales
All credit sales and sales above a set amount have numbered documents
All sales are documented in number order and checked against the ledger

evidence.requirement: Inspect the invoice or receipt books for sequence and compare with the ledger.

questions.text: The three most important routine tasks (for example cash handling, receiving goods, processing orders) each have written steps.
anchors: None are written or explained
Steps are known verbally only
One task has written steps
All three tasks have written steps
All three are written, staff are trained on them and they were updated in the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Ask for the three step lists and ask a staff member to describe one.

questions.text: Someone other than the owner can find and read the main business records.
anchors: Only the owner knows where records are and how they work
Only the owner can use the records
One trusted person knows where they are
A named records person has access and can use them
A written index exists and two people have been trained to use the records

evidence.requirement: Ask a second person to find a stated record while the owner is not helping.
examples: Bookkeeper retrieves last month's ledger unaided
Index sheet to the filing system

questions.riskTag: Records known only to the owner

questions.text: Share of sales receipts that go through mobile money or a bank account.
anchors: Under 10 percent
10 to 29 percent
30 to 49 percent
50 to 79 percent
80 percent or more

evidence.requirement: Compare digital receipts on statements with total sales in the same month.

questions.riskTag: Most sales are in untraceable cash

questions.text: The business has a bank account or mobile money business wallet in the business's name that is in regular use.
anchors: No account or wallet in the business's name
Account or wallet exists but has no transactions in the last three months
Account or wallet in the business's name shows transactions in each of the last three months

evidence.requirement: Review statements from the last three months in the business's name.

questions.text: Sales and accounts are kept in a spreadsheet or software, not only on paper or in the owner's head.
anchors: Nothing is kept in any digital form
Notes on a phone only
Spreadsheet used occasionally
Spreadsheet or software used for the ledger every month
Accounting or point of sale software with backups, and reports used every month

evidence.requirement: Open the file or software and check entries and dates.

questions.text: Customers can reach the business through a dedicated business phone number, WhatsApp Business or email address.
anchors: No way for customers to reach the business except by visiting
Only the owner's personal number is available
A business number exists but is not displayed
A dedicated number or email is displayed on signage, cards or social media
Dedicated contact is displayed and enquiries are answered within a set time and logged

evidence.requirement: Check signage, social media page and send a test enquiry.
examples: Banner showing the business phone number

questions.text: The business tracks a small set of numbers every month (sales, gross margin, cash balance, money owed by customers, stock).
anchors: No numbers are tracked
Sales only
Sales and cash
Four or more measures in writing every month
Monthly dashboard with targets and a trend over six months

evidence.requirement: Ask for the last three months' figures.

questions.text: In the last six months the owner has made a decision that was clearly based on the recorded figures.
anchors: Decisions are made by gut feeling alone
Records exist but are not consulted
The owner occasionally looks at figures
Two decisions in the last six months can be traced to the figures
Figures are used routinely and decisions are written with the numbers behind them

evidence.requirement: Ask for two decisions and the figures used, and check dates.
examples: Dropped a slow product after stock figures
Raised a price after margin calculation

questions.text: The owner compares this year's results with last year's at least once a year.
anchors: No records to compare
Compares from memory only
Compares sales only
Compares sales, costs and profit once a year
Compares every quarter and writes down the reasons for changes

evidence.requirement: Ask for the comparison and the reasons noted.
examples: Year on year sales and costs table

questions.text: At least each quarter, actual results are compared with the plan or budget and the differences are explained in writing.
anchors: Never compared
Compared informally once a year
Compared informally each quarter
Written comparison each quarter
Written comparison each month with corrective actions closed

evidence.requirement: Ask for the last two comparisons and the actions that followed.

questions.text: The business is legally registered and its registration is current (certificate valid, annual renewal or annual return up to date).
anchors: Not registered with the Registrar General's Department
Registered, but the annual renewal or annual return is overdue or the details are out of date
Valid certificate in the business's name, with annual renewal or annual return up to date

evidence.requirement: Inspect the certificate and the latest renewal or annual return acknowledgement.
examples: Business name or company registration certificate
Registrar General annual return or renewal receipt

questions.text: All tax returns that fell due in the last 12 months have been filed on time with the Ghana Revenue Authority.
anchors: No TIN, or no returns have been filed
Has a TIN but has filed no returns
Some returns have been filed
All returns have been filed but some were late
All returns filed on time, with GRA acknowledgements kept

evidence.requirement: Ask for the TIN and filing acknowledgements, and check dates against due dates.

questions.riskTag: Tax returns not filed on time

questions.text: The owner can say which GRA taxes apply to the business (income tax, VAT, PAYE, withholding) and keeps a calendar of due dates.
anchors: Unaware which taxes apply
Knows only about income tax
Knows the main taxes but has no calendar
Has a calendar of the taxes that apply, with due dates
Calendar kept, payments tracked with receipts, and advice taken from a tax practitioner or GRA

evidence.requirement: Ask for the calendar and the payment receipts for the last quarter.
examples: Tax calendar on the office wall
Spreadsheet of tax due dates and payment dates

questions.text: Employee SSNIT contributions and PAYE are paid by the due date every month.
anchors: Employees are not registered with SSNIT and PAYE is not deducted
Registered but contributions are in arrears
Paid, but often late
Paid on time in most months, with proof
Paid on time every month for 12 months, with SSNIT and GRA proof

evidence.requirement: Ask for SSNIT contribution schedules, payment proof and PAYE payment evidence for the last six months.

questions.text: Important sales and supply arrangements (large customers, key suppliers, premises) are in written agreements.
anchors: No written agreements
Everything is verbal
Some arrangements are in messages or notes only
Written, signed agreements exist for large buyers and key suppliers
Signed agreements cover price, payment, delivery and ending the contract, and are filed and reviewed

evidence.requirement: Ask for the agreements with the three largest customers or suppliers.

questions.text: The business has a right to use its premises for at least the next 12 months, shown in a lease, tenancy agreement or title.
anchors: No right to the premises and a risk of being moved
A verbal arrangement only
A written agreement exists but expires within six months
A written lease or tenancy valid for at least 12 months
Title, or a lease of three years or more

evidence.requirement: Inspect the lease, tenancy agreement or title document and check dates.

questions.text: The business has taken a step to stop its brand name, logo or product design being copied.
anchors: Unaware this is possible and copying has occurred
Aware but has done nothing
Business name registered only
Trademark or design application filed, or staff have signed confidentiality terms
Trademark or design granted, or confidentiality is in force and breaches are handled

evidence.requirement: Ask for the registration, application or signed confidentiality terms.

questions.text: The owner has written a list of the main risks to the business (fire, theft, price changes, loss of a key customer, illness) and what will be done about each.
anchors: Has not thought about risks
Aware of risks but nothing is discussed or written
An informal list exists
A written list names the main risks, an owner and an action for each
Written list reviewed at least yearly and after any incident, with actions checked

evidence.requirement: Ask for the risk list and the last review date.
examples: Notebook page of risks and responses

questions.text: The business holds valid insurance for its biggest insurable risks (stock, premises, vehicles, workers).
anchors: No insurance of any kind
Knows the options but holds none
Holds only compulsory cover such as vehicle third party
Main assets and stock are insured with valid policies
Valid policies with values checked at least yearly

evidence.requirement: Inspect the policy documents, the cover amounts and the expiry dates.

questions.text: Valuable stock and cash are protected by physical controls (locks, safe, limited keyholders, cash banked regularly).
anchors: Stock and cash are left exposed
Locked at night only
Locked, with some limits on who has access
Secured storage with a limited number of keyholders and cash banked at least weekly
As before, plus daily banking and a record of access and incidents

evidence.requirement: Inspect storage, ask who holds keys and check banking dates.

questions.riskTag: Stock and cash exposed to theft

questions.text: Written steps exist for keeping key activities running after a disruption (fire, power cut, illness of a key person, loss of premises).
anchors: No plan of any kind
Owner has a plan in mind only
Informal notes for one scenario
A written plan for the main disruptions with a contact list
Written plan tested or practised within the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Ask for the plan and any record of a practice or real use.
examples: Notes from a power cut drill

questions.text: Business records and customer data are backed up so they could be recovered after loss of a phone, computer or the premises.
anchors: No backup; one copy only
A second copy is kept in the same place
Occasional backups with no routine
Monthly backup kept in a separate place (cloud, other premises) and recovery within a week is possible
At least weekly off site backup and a recovery test done in the last 12 months, recovering within a day

evidence.requirement: Ask to see the backup and the date of the last one, and ask for a test restore.
examples: External drive with dated copies kept off site

questions.text: The business handles personal data about customers and staff in line with the Data Protection Act, including registration with the Data Protection Commission.
anchors: Unaware of the rules; personal data is on open or shared phones and papers
Aware of the rules but has taken no steps
Basic security (lock, passcodes) but not registered
Registered with the Data Protection Commission and basic security in place
Registration renewed, written data handling rules, staff briefed and a way to answer data requests

evidence.requirement: Ask for the registration certificate and inspect how personal data is stored.
examples: Locked cabinet for staff files and password protected customer list

questions.riskTag: Personal data not protected or registered

questions.text: Electricity, fuel and water use and cost are tracked every month.
anchors: Not tracked
Bills are paid but not compared
Bills are kept and total cost is known
Monthly cost is compared and the biggest users are identified
Units used are tracked against output and a reduction target is set

evidence.requirement: Ask for the last six months of utility bills and the comparison.
examples: ECG electricity bills and prepaid meter records

questions.riskTag: Energy and water use not tracked

questions.text: In the last 12 months the business has taken at least one action to cut energy or water use (LED lighting, solar, efficient equipment, repairing leaks).
anchors: No action and none planned
An action is being considered
One low cost action has been taken
Two or more actions taken and savings estimated
Savings measured and further actions planned

evidence.requirement: Inspect the measures and compare bills before and after.
examples: Solar panel or LED bulbs installed

questions.text: Waste (packaging, scrap, used oil, chemicals, electronic waste, organic waste) is sorted, reused or disposed of safely.
anchors: Waste is dumped or burnt in the open
Left for general collection with no separation
Some waste is reused or collected
Waste is sorted, reused or sold, and hazardous items go to an approved collector
As before, with waste measured and reduced

evidence.requirement: Inspect waste handling and ask for collector or buyer receipts for hazardous or recyclable items.
examples: Separate bins for scrap and plastics

questions.text: The business has taken a practical step against a climate hazard that affects it (flood, heat, drought, storm, power outages).
anchors: Has not considered climate hazards
Has considered them but done nothing
Has a plan but not yet acted
One practical step is in place, such as drainage, shade, water storage or backup power
Several steps in place and reviewed after each event

evidence.requirement: Inspect the measure and ask what hazard it addresses and when it was done.
examples: Backup power supply for a cold room

questions.text: Women and men doing the same work in the business are paid equally and have the same chance of promotion.
anchors: Clear pay gaps or exclusion from promotion
Inequality is known and accepted
No rule on equal pay, but no known gap
Pay scales are the same for the same role and have been checked
Pay and role data by gender are reviewed yearly and gaps acted on

evidence.requirement: Compare pay for the same role across women and men and ask staff about promotion.
examples: Promotion decisions in the last two years

questions.text: Both women and people under 35 hold jobs with real responsibility (supervisor, technician, manager), not only casual or lowest paid roles.
anchors: Neither group holds any role of responsibility, or any role at all
Both groups work only in casual or lowest paid roles
One of the two groups holds a role of responsibility
Both groups hold at least one role of responsibility
Both groups hold several such roles and a training or apprenticeship route is recorded

evidence.requirement: Review the staff list by role, sex and age band and ask about training routes.
examples: Staff list showing supervisors by sex and age

questions.riskTag: Women and youth excluded from responsibility

questions.text: Women who own, work in or help run the business take part in decisions about how its income is spent.
anchors: Women have no say in decisions
Women are consulted rarely
Women are consulted but the owner decides alone
Women take part in business decisions that affect them
Women confirm, when asked separately, that they take part in decisions and control the income they earn

evidence.requirement: Speak separately to the women connected to the business about their role in decisions and income.
examples: Wife or female partner confirms joint decisions on spending
Female staff describe how bonuses and tasks are decided

questions.text: The workplace has a rule against harassment and a safe way for staff to report it.
anchors: No rule and harassment is tolerated
A verbal rule only
An informal open door with the owner
A written rule known to staff, with a named person to report to
Written rule, staff briefed, and a reporting process that is used and logged

evidence.requirement: Ask for the written rule and ask two staff how they would report a concern.
examples: Notice naming the person to report to

questions.riskTag: No harassment rule or reporting route

questions.text: The owner has written down what the business would do if monthly sales fell by a quarter for three months.
anchors: Has no idea what would be done
Would cut staff or borrow personally, with no plan
Actions are described verbally
A written response with triggers and cost cuts
Written response that has been rehearsed or used before

evidence.requirement: Ask for the written response and when it was last reviewed.
examples: Page of cost cuts and triggers
Plan used during a previous sales drop

questions.riskTag: No plan for a sales drop

questions.text: Share of sales in the last 12 months that came from the largest single product or service line.
anchors: Above 90 percent
76 to 90 percent
61 to 75 percent
41 to 60 percent
40 percent or less

evidence.requirement: Calculate from sales records by product or service line.

questions.text: The owner belongs to a business association, cooperative, trade group or peer network and has attended its meetings.
anchors: Not a member of any network and works alone
Member but not active
Attended one meeting in the last six months
Attended two or more meetings in the last six months
Active, and has used the network for a concrete benefit in the last 12 months (referral, shared purchase, guarantee)

evidence.requirement: Ask for membership proof and a recent benefit received.

questions.text: At least two people can perform each critical task (taking orders, bookkeeping, production, delivery).
anchors: Each task depends on one person and nobody can cover
Informal cover for some tasks only
Backup named for one critical task
Backups named for all critical tasks
Backups named and tested through cross training in the last 12 months

evidence.requirement: Ask who covers each critical task and when cover was last used.
examples: Second person trained to do invoicing

questions.riskTag: Critical tasks depend on one person

mapping.gapPattern: Plans live in the owner's head or on loose paper, have no cedi targets, and staff cannot say what they are aiming for. Big purchases are made without a payback calculation.
mapping.diagnosis: The business is steered by instinct, so growth is reactive and spending on equipment or stock is not tested against expected return.
mapping.prescription: Write a one page 12 month plan with sales, gross margin and profit targets by quarter, share the targets with the team, and use a payback sheet before any purchase above an agreed cedi limit.

intervention.resources: One page annual plan template, payback calculator sheet, three coaching sessions

measurement.kpi: Quarters with a written target reviewed against actual results
measurement.baselineMethod: Inspect current plan and last large purchase calculation at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: Written plan with numeric targets in place and two quarterly reviews held within six months

mapping.gapPattern: Owner believes customers are loyal but cannot name repeat buyers, has not asked why they buy and cannot state what makes the business different.
mapping.diagnosis: Demand is assumed rather than evidenced, which makes sales fragile and weakens any case to a lender, buyer or investor.
mapping.prescription: Keep a simple customer record, call ten recent customers to ask why they buy and what they would change, write the main reason customers choose the business, and make one change from the feedback within 60 days.

intervention.resources: Customer record template, ten question call guide, coach visit to review findings

measurement.kpi: Repeat customers in the last six months, from the customer record
measurement.baselineMethod: Count customers who bought in at least two of the last six months from records
measurement.provisionalTarget: Customer record in use and repeat customer count up by 20 percent
measurement.dataSource: Customer ledger or mobile money history

mapping.gapPattern: New customers come by chance, there is no contact list, one buyer takes most of the sales and nobody knows which channel works.
mapping.diagnosis: Sales growth is unplanned and concentrated, so the loss of a single buyer would threaten the business.
mapping.prescription: Build a customer contact list, write a six month plan to win five new buyers, count new customers by source each month, and set a ceiling for the share any one buyer can take.

intervention.resources: WhatsApp Business setup guide, new buyer pipeline sheet, marketing source tally sheet

measurement.kpi: Largest customer's share of sales and number of new customers per month
measurement.baselineMethod: Calculate from the last 12 months of sales records
measurement.provisionalTarget: Largest customer under 40 percent of sales and at least two new customers per month
measurement.dataSource: Sales ledger and new customer tally

mapping.gapPattern: Prices are copied from the next trader or guessed, competitors are rarely checked and discounts are given on request without limit.
mapping.diagnosis: Prices may not cover true cost, so margins are eroded without the owner realising.
mapping.prescription: Cost the top five products or services, set prices as cost plus a target margin, compare with three competitors twice a year and write a discount limit that staff follow.

intervention.resources: SIYB style costing exercise, pricing sheet template, competitor price comparison form

measurement.kpi: Share of main items priced from a written cost sheet
measurement.baselineMethod: Review costing sheets for the five best selling items
measurement.provisionalTarget: All five main items priced from a cost sheet and reviewed at least once

mapping.gapPattern: Orders are sometimes late or wrong, complaints are handled from memory, there is no checklist and different staff produce different results.
mapping.diagnosis: Quality and delivery depend on individuals, which risks losing buyers and prevents access to demanding markets.
mapping.prescription: Write a quality checklist for the main product, keep a complaints and returns book, record promised and actual delivery dates and review results weekly.

intervention.resources: Quality checklist, delivery log template, complaints register, on site visit to map the process

measurement.kpi: On time and correct delivery rate, and complaints per 100 orders
measurement.baselineMethod: Count one month of orders from the order book and complaints notes
measurement.provisionalTarget: On time and correct rate of at least 90 percent, with complaints logged and closed

mapping.gapPattern: Stock is not counted, one supplier is relied on, losses are guessed and cost rises are noticed only when cash runs short.
mapping.diagnosis: Leakage through loss, theft and unnoticed price rises is reducing margin and the business is exposed to supply failure.
mapping.prescription: Count stock monthly against a stock book, record losses for the main item, name two suppliers per key input and compare monthly cost lines.

intervention.resources: Stock book, monthly count sheet, loss record, supplier comparison sheet

measurement.kpi: Stock count variance percent and loss percent for the main item
measurement.baselineMethod: Do a physical count and compare with the book, and estimate losses from the last month
measurement.provisionalTarget: Monthly counts held, variance under 5 percent and losses recorded for three months
measurement.dataSource: Stock count sheets and loss record

mapping.gapPattern: Equipment is repaired only after it breaks, there is no asset list, output is not counted and one step always delays orders.
mapping.diagnosis: Avoidable downtime and an unmeasured work process limit capacity and weaken collateral and insurance cases.
mapping.prescription: Create an asset register, set a service schedule for key machines and vehicles, count output weekly and tackle the main bottleneck.

intervention.resources: Asset register template, maintenance schedule, process walk through and bottleneck review

measurement.kpi: Unplanned downtime days per month and output per worker per week
measurement.baselineMethod: Record downtime and output for four weeks
measurement.provisionalTarget: Asset register complete, service schedule followed and downtime reduced by a third

mapping.gapPattern: Money in and out is not written down, personal and business money are mixed, receipts are loose and the ledger is months behind.
mapping.diagnosis: The owner cannot show what the business earns or owes, which blocks lender and funder trust and hides losses.
mapping.prescription: Open a separate business account or wallet, start a weekly cash book, file receipts monthly and set a fixed owner pay.

intervention.resources: Simple cash book, filing box and monthly folders, owner pay agreement, two bookkeeping sessions and weekly check ins

measurement.kpi: Weeks in the last 12 with complete cash book entries
measurement.baselineMethod: Inspect the cash book and statements for the last eight weeks
measurement.provisionalTarget: At least 24 of the next 26 weeks complete, with no unrecorded personal withdrawals
measurement.dataSource: Cash book and mobile money or bank statements

mapping.gapPattern: The owner does not know how many weeks of costs cash can cover, there is no forecast and customers pay late.
mapping.diagnosis: Cash shortages are managed by crisis borrowing, which makes the business vulnerable to even small shocks.
mapping.prescription: Count cash weekly, build a four week cash forecast, agree payment terms in writing, chase debtors weekly and build a cash buffer of at least four weeks of fixed costs.

intervention.resources: Four week cash forecast template, debtors list, debtor chasing script, weekly coaching call

measurement.kpi: Weeks of fixed costs covered by cash, and debtor days
measurement.baselineMethod: Add balances on the day and divide by weekly fixed costs; compute debtor days from the debtors list
measurement.provisionalTarget: Cash cover at least four weeks and debtor days under 45
measurement.dataSource: Cash balances, debtors list and fixed cost list

mapping.gapPattern: Margins are guessed, the break even point is unknown and profit is judged by whether there is cash in hand.
mapping.diagnosis: The owner cannot tell which products pay, so effort and capital go to items that may lose money.
mapping.prescription: Calculate gross margin per main item, work out monthly break even and calculate net profit after owner pay for the last year.

intervention.resources: Margin per product worksheet, break even calculator, profit and loss template

measurement.kpi: Gross margin percent per main product and monthly net profit
measurement.baselineMethod: Compute from the last three months of records
measurement.provisionalTarget: Margins known for all main items and net profit tracked monthly for six months

mapping.gapPattern: No annual financial statements, one person records and handles all money, payments need no approval and balances are never reconciled.
mapping.diagnosis: Weak controls leave the business open to error and fraud and cannot satisfy lenders or grant makers who need accountable financial reports.
mapping.prescription: Engage a bookkeeper or accountant to prepare statements, set a payment approval limit, reconcile cash, bank and mobile money monthly with a second person and file monthly management accounts.

intervention.resources: Accountant or bookkeeper engagement, reconciliation template, payment voucher book, internal control checklist

measurement.kpi: Months with a completed reconciliation, and statements prepared
measurement.baselineMethod: Inspect last statements and reconciliations at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: Six consecutive monthly reconciliations and annual statements prepared

mapping.gapPattern: Repayments are sometimes late, the total debt is not known, loans pay for routine bills and repayments are not covered by cash surplus.
mapping.diagnosis: Debt is straining cash flow and the business is at risk of default, which would damage its credit record.
mapping.prescription: List all debts with due dates, work out monthly debt cover, restructure or stop non productive borrowing and set up a repayment reserve account.

intervention.resources: Debt list template, debt cover calculator, repayment reserve account, lender engagement support

measurement.kpi: Debt cover ratio and number of late repayments
measurement.baselineMethod: Compute from loan schedules and monthly cash surplus
measurement.provisionalTarget: Debt cover of at least 1.5 times and no late repayments for six months

mapping.gapPattern: The owner has never seen their credit report, may have unresolved arrears, has no regular savings and has little history of complete applications.
mapping.diagnosis: Finance access is limited by an unknown or weak credit record and thin application experience.
mapping.prescription: Obtain and check the credit report, clear and document any arrears, save a fixed amount monthly into a business account or group, and prepare one complete application using lender feedback.

intervention.resources: Credit bureau enquiry, savings plan template, lender introduction, application checklist

measurement.kpi: Clean credit report on file and months of regular business saving
measurement.baselineMethod: Obtain the credit report and savings statements at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: Credit report checked, errors resolved, and six months of regular saving

mapping.gapPattern: The business has no funding plan or projections, ownership is not documented and information for funders takes weeks to assemble.
mapping.diagnosis: Even a bankable business may fail to attract funding because it cannot present itself credibly.
mapping.prescription: Build a one page funding request, a 12 month projection with assumptions, an ownership record, and a ready information folder that can be sent within one day.

intervention.resources: Funding request template, projection model, funder information folder checklist, review by a consultant

measurement.kpi: Funder information folder completeness and time to assemble
measurement.baselineMethod: Ask the owner to assemble the folder and time it
measurement.provisionalTarget: Folder complete and assembled in under one working day

mapping.gapPattern: Everything stops when the owner is away, no deputy is named and the owner has no time for planning or learning.
mapping.diagnosis: The business is a one person dependency and cannot grow, borrow or be sold.
mapping.prescription: Name a deputy, write a handover note, delegate three recurring decisions, and block a weekly planning hour.

intervention.resources: Delegation checklist, handover note template, deputy briefing sessions, weekly planning slot

measurement.kpi: Days the business ran without the owner and decisions delegated
measurement.baselineMethod: Ask the owner and deputy about the last absence
measurement.provisionalTarget: Deputy named in writing and one week run without the owner with no loss

mapping.gapPattern: Roles are unwritten, new staff learn by watching, good performance is not recognised and nobody knows why people leave.
mapping.diagnosis: Weak role clarity and no recognition leads to errors, low motivation and costly turnover.
mapping.prescription: Write roles for each person, run induction for new starters, introduce clear and fair recognition criteria and record reasons for leaving.

intervention.resources: Role description template, induction checklist, simple recognition rules, staff register

measurement.kpi: Share of staff with a written role and staff turnover in 12 months
measurement.baselineMethod: Count written roles and leavers in the last 12 months
measurement.provisionalTarget: All staff with a written role and induction used for every new starter

mapping.gapPattern: No regular management meeting, nobody outside the business challenges decisions and staff do not know what they may decide.
mapping.diagnosis: Decisions rest on one person, which weakens accountability and funder confidence.
mapping.prescription: Hold a monthly review with minutes, form a small advisory group with at least one independent person, and write a delegation of authority sheet.

intervention.resources: Meeting minute template, advisory group terms of reference, delegation of authority sheet

measurement.kpi: Monthly reviews held with minutes and advisory meetings held
measurement.baselineMethod: Inspect minutes for the last six months
measurement.provisionalTarget: Six monthly reviews with minutes and two advisory meetings in six months

mapping.gapPattern: Staff have no written terms and the workplace has unchecked hazards, no first aid and no incident record.
mapping.diagnosis: The business risks legal exposure, injuries, disputes and loss of grant or buyer eligibility.
mapping.prescription: Issue written contracts to all employees, set up first aid and fire safety, and keep an incident book reviewed quarterly.

intervention.resources: Employment contract template, safety walk through checklist, first aid kit, incident book

measurement.kpi: Employees with a signed written statement of terms and recorded safety checks
measurement.baselineMethod: Sample contracts and inspect safety measures at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: All employees with written terms and quarterly safety checks recorded
measurement.dataSource: Contract file and safety check records

mapping.gapPattern: Key papers are scattered, sales have no receipts, routine tasks are not written down and only the owner can find records.
mapping.diagnosis: The business cannot prove its transactions or hand over operations, which weakens compliance and lender confidence.
mapping.prescription: Set up one document file with an index, issue numbered receipts for all sales above an agreed amount, write steps for three routine tasks and train a second person on the records.

intervention.resources: Document file and index sheet, numbered receipt books, procedure templates

measurement.kpi: Key documents found within ten minutes and share of sales with a receipt
measurement.baselineMethod: Ask for five named documents and sample ten sales
measurement.provisionalTarget: All key documents found in ten minutes and over 90 percent of sales receipted

mapping.gapPattern: Most receipts are cash, there is no business account or wallet, accounts are on paper only and customers can reach the business only through the owner's phone.
mapping.diagnosis: Untraceable money and a lack of digital records limit credit access and slow the business down.
mapping.prescription: Open a business account or merchant wallet, move customer payments to digital channels, set up a spreadsheet or basic accounting app and publish a business contact number.

intervention.resources: Merchant wallet or business account opening support, spreadsheet ledger template, WhatsApp Business setup

measurement.kpi: Share of sales received through mobile money or bank
measurement.baselineMethod: Compare digital receipts with total sales for the last month
measurement.provisionalTarget: At least 50 percent of sales received digitally and a business wallet in regular use
measurement.dataSource: Mobile money or bank statements and sales ledger

mapping.gapPattern: Few or no numbers are tracked, decisions are made by feel and results are never compared with last year or with a plan.
mapping.diagnosis: Management is blind to trends, so problems are found late.
mapping.prescription: Choose five monthly key numbers, build a one page monthly scorecard, review it with the team and compare actual results with plan each quarter.

intervention.resources: Monthly scorecard template, quarterly budget versus actual sheet, coaching reviews

measurement.kpi: Months with a completed scorecard
measurement.baselineMethod: Inspect scorecards or notes for the last three months
measurement.provisionalTarget: Six consecutive monthly scorecards and two quarterly plan comparisons

mapping.gapPattern: Registration is not current, returns are filed late or not at all, the owner does not know which taxes apply and SSNIT or PAYE is in arrears.
mapping.diagnosis: The business is exposed to penalties and is ineligible for contracts, loans and grants that require registration and tax clearance.
mapping.prescription: Renew or complete registration with the Registrar General, file outstanding GRA returns, set a tax calendar and clear or schedule SSNIT and PAYE arrears.

intervention.resources: Registrar General and GRA portal support, tax calendar template, tax practitioner engagement, SSNIT payment plan

measurement.kpi: Compliance items current out of registration, returns, SSNIT and PAYE
measurement.baselineMethod: Check each item against certificates, acknowledgements and schedules
measurement.provisionalTarget: All applicable items current within six months
measurement.dataSource: Certificates, GRA acknowledgements and SSNIT reports

mapping.gapPattern: Agreements with buyers and suppliers are verbal, premises are insecure and the brand has no protection.
mapping.diagnosis: The business has weak recourse in disputes and could lose premises or its brand.
mapping.prescription: Put agreements with the largest buyers and suppliers in writing, secure a lease or tenancy for at least 12 months, and record the business name and brand.

intervention.resources: Simple supply agreement template, lease review, brand registration guidance

measurement.kpi: Written agreements held with top three buyers and suppliers
measurement.baselineMethod: Count signed agreements at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: Signed agreements with the top three buyers and suppliers and a 12 month lease

mapping.gapPattern: There is no risk list, stock and assets are uninsured and stock and cash are poorly secured.
mapping.diagnosis: A single fire, theft or loss could end the business with no recovery route.
mapping.prescription: Write a risk list with a response for each main risk, buy insurance for stock and premises, and secure stock and cash with locks and regular banking.

intervention.resources: Risk register template, insurance broker introduction, storage security checklist

measurement.kpi: Main risks with a named response and insurance policies in force
measurement.baselineMethod: Review risk list and policies at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: Risk list complete and insurance on stock and premises in force

mapping.gapPattern: There is no continuity plan, records have one copy and personal data is held without safeguards or registration.
mapping.diagnosis: A disruption or data loss could stop operations and expose the business to legal action.
mapping.prescription: Write a continuity plan for the three most likely disruptions, set up monthly backups off site, and register with the Data Protection Commission and lock personal data.

intervention.resources: Continuity checklist, cloud backup setup, Data Protection Commission registration support

measurement.kpi: Continuity plan in place, backup age in days and registration status
measurement.baselineMethod: Check plan, last backup date and registration certificate
measurement.provisionalTarget: Plan written, weekly backups running and registration complete

mapping.gapPattern: Energy and water use are untracked, waste is dumped and no action has been taken against climate hazards.
mapping.diagnosis: Avoidable resource costs and exposure to flood, heat or power cuts are eroding margin and resilience.
mapping.prescription: Track utility use monthly, take two low cost saving actions, set up safe waste handling and make one climate hazard adjustment.

intervention.resources: Utility tracking sheet, resource efficiency walk through, waste handling guidance

measurement.kpi: Monthly utility cost per unit of output
measurement.baselineMethod: Compute from six months of bills and output records
measurement.provisionalTarget: Utility cost per unit down by 10 percent and waste sorted

mapping.gapPattern: Pay and promotion differ by sex without clear reason, women and young people hold only the lowest roles and there is no harassment rule.
mapping.diagnosis: The business is losing talent and may be exposed to legal and donor risk.
mapping.prescription: Review pay by role and sex, open a path to responsibility for women and young people, hear women's views on decisions and write a harassment rule with a reporting route.

intervention.resources: Pay by role review sheet, harassment policy template, staff briefing session

measurement.kpi: Pay gap by role and share of women and young people in responsible roles
measurement.baselineMethod: Analyse the payroll and staff list at assessment
measurement.provisionalTarget: No unexplained pay gap, harassment rule issued and staff briefed

mapping.gapPattern: There is no plan for a sales drop, one product earns almost all income, the owner is isolated and critical tasks have no cover.
mapping.diagnosis: The business has little buffer against shocks and has few adaptation options.
mapping.prescription: Write a sales drop response, test a second product or service, join a trade group or peer network and train a second person on each critical task.

intervention.resources: Stress test worksheet, peer group sessions, cross training plan

measurement.kpi: Share of sales from the largest product line and critical tasks with a trained backup
measurement.baselineMethod: Compute from sales by product and list critical tasks
measurement.provisionalTarget: Largest product line under 60 percent of sales and backups for all critical tasks

readiness.name: Bank finance readiness
readiness.purpose: Shows whether a lender would find the business bankable: reliable cash records, separate money, repayment history, current registration and tax status, and a business account.
readiness.unlocks: Not ready or Emerging: fix the blocking gate items first (cash book, separate accounts, reconciliation, registration, tax filing). Ready: prepare the funder information pack and approach a bank or microfinance lender with a costed request.

readiness.name: Market and buyer readiness
readiness.purpose: Shows whether the business can supply a larger or more demanding buyer: proven repeat demand, reliable delivery, quality control, tax compliance, written terms and traceable sales documents.
readiness.unlocks: Not ready or Emerging: build delivery reliability, quality checks and evidence of repeat buyers. Ready: pitch to institutional, wholesale or contract buyers who require tax clearance and written agreements.

readiness.name: Investment readiness (equity, impact or blended capital)
readiness.purpose: Shows whether the business could stand up to investor due diligence: evidenced demand, financial statements, documented ownership, margin and projection discipline, and owner independence.
readiness.unlocks: Not ready or Emerging: close the gate items (demand evidence, records, statements, ownership) and the owner dependence gap. Ready: begin investor conversations with a pitch pack and projections.

readiness.name: Grant and donor readiness
readiness.purpose: Shows whether the business can receive and account for grant money: financial controls, reconciliation, registration, workable governance, safety and inclusion practices.
readiness.unlocks: Not ready or Emerging: put in place financial controls, reconciliation, a business account and registration. Ready: apply to donor and development programmes and bid for cofinanced support.

readiness.name: Statutory compliance readiness
readiness.purpose: Shows whether the business meets its basic legal duties: registration, tax filing, SSNIT and PAYE, written employment terms, safety, data protection and documented ownership.
readiness.unlocks: Not ready or Emerging: clear registration, filing and SSNIT arrears with a compliance calendar. Ready: apply for tenders, licences, supplier listings and programmes that require compliance evidence.

consistencyChecks.rule: If cash and mobile money are recorded at least weekly, sales and purchases should also be recorded in a ledger. High on one and very low on the other suggests inflated answers or records that are not real.
A net profit worked out from records cannot be credible if cash and mobile money are not recorded.
Prices set from a written cost sheet imply the gross margin is known for the main items.
Tax returns cannot be filed on time if the business has no registration; check which answer is wrong.
Loans reported as repaid on time should be consistent with no unresolved default or blacklisting.
Business money kept separate from household money implies the money in and out of the business is written down.
A funder information pack ready within a day implies supporting documents are filed and traceable.
Monthly key numbers cannot be reliable if sales and purchases are not recorded in a ledger.
A business that runs for a week without the owner should have written limits on what staff may decide.
